newsitem.title: PERU: Judge only hostage killed in Peru assault - congressman.
newsitem.headline: Judge only hostage killed in Peru assault - congressman.

text.p: Peruvian troops stormed the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima on Tuesday, freeing 71 hostages held by Marxist rebels, but one captive, a supreme court judge, was killed, a government congressman said.

Congressman Daniel Espichan told Reuters judge Carlos Giusti Acuna was the only hostage killed in a brief but fierce battle between troops and about 20 Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas who had held the building for 126 days.
Local radio and television said all the guerrillas were also killed in the assault.
An ecstatic President Alberto Fujimori yelled to crowds lining the streets later that all the hostages were "safe and sound" despite the reports that one had died.
Reuters correspondents at the scene counted at least 60 of the 72 captives leaving safely.
Masked soldiers waved assault rifles in the air, cheered, sang the national anthem and punched their fists in the air after the 40-minute operation to end Latin America's longest hostage siege.
Fujimori, wearing a bullet-proof jacket, arrived at the site immediately afterwards and entered the compound where he was cheered by soldiers.

They swarmed into the building from private houses behind the diplomatic compound at 3.20 P.M. (2020 GMT) and engaged about 20 MRTA rebels in a battle punctuated by billowing smoke, gunfire and explosions and shown live on television.
At about 4 P.M. they triumphantly pulled down the MRTA flag that had flown over the residence since it was stormed in an audacious raid during a glamorous cocktail party on Dec. 17.
The freed hostages included Peruvian Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela and Japanese ambassador Morihisa Aoki as well as other senior government officials.
At least five hostages were injured, four of them carried out on stretchers. Seven policemen were also injured, witnesses said.
MRTA spokesman Isaac Velazco told Reuters from Hamburg by telephone that the guerrillas would retaliate for the assault by attacking military and economic targets in Peru.
Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said he was given no warning of the assault but thanked the Peruvian government for freeing the hostages, including all 24 Japanese captives.
The storming of the residence came after negotations between the Peruvian government and rebels -- mainly through a three-man guarantors committee -- had failed to bring a breakthrough.
Fujimori faced the worst crisis of his turbulent seven years in office over the hostage seizure.
The MRTA wanted the release of jailed comrades, a demand the government had always rejected.

The Cuban-inspired MRTA is the smallest of Peru's two main rebel movements. Violent conflicts unleashed by it and the larger Shining Path movement have cost 30,000 lives and $25 billion in infrastructure damage in Peru since 1980.
After Tuesday's raid, pale, fraught-looking relatives and friends of the hostages gathered outside the Lima Police Hospital where they were taken.
The United States said the guerrillas bore full responsibility for the storming of the building.
U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen said Washington had no official advance warning of the move and had taken no part in what he called a "responsible" action by Peru.
